stimuli.text: Researchers want to investigate whether a brief mindfulness exercise before tests improves scores. They have 80 students in a statistics class available.

Random samples of 15 were taken from two groups. The values of reaction time (hundredths of a second) are:

**Morning:** 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 16, 16, 16, 20, 21, 21, 24, 26, 28, 30

**Evening:** 15, 17, 18, 20, 21, 21, 21, 25, 26, 33, 33, 33, 38, 45, 60
A school district claims that 40% of its students take public transit to school. A reporter suspects the true proportion is higher. In a random sample of 350 students, 165 take public transit.

Data were collected on age of car (years) (x) and price (thousands of dollars) (y) for a sample of used cars. A scatterplot shows a linear pattern, and the residual plot shows no pattern. Computer output for the least-squares regression is shown.

```text
Predictor   Coef      SE Coef
Constant    15.9
x           -1.2
S = 4.1    R-Sq = 89.0%
```

questions.stem: A point with an x value far from the others noticeably changes the slope when removed. What is it?

options.text: A point with a residual of 0
options.why: Influence is about leverage, not residual size.
The line always passes through it.
Correct. Removing it changes the regression line substantially.
That is a variable, not a point.

questions.explanation: Removing it changes the regression line substantially.

questions.stem: Two independent random samples have n₁ = 25, s₁ = 11 and n₂ = 56, s₂ = 19. What is the standard error of x̄₁ − x̄₂?

options.why: Each sample contributes s²/n.
Add variances, then take the square root; standard errors do not add.
Variances add, even for a difference.
Correct. √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂).

questions.stem: Each of 20 students takes a reading test before and after a summer program. Which procedure compares the scores?

options.why: Scores are quantitative.
The samples are not independent.
That is for categorical data.

options.text: A paired t procedure on the differences (after − before)
options.why: Correct. Two measurements on the same students are paired.

questions.explanation: Two measurements on the same students are paired.

questions.stem: A student is chosen at random from those who drive to school. What is the probability the student is a junior?

options.why: That is P(drives | junior).
Correct. P(junior | drives) = juniors who drive ÷ all who drive.
That is P(junior and drives); divide by drivers only.
That is P(junior) overall.

questions.stem: A variable is approximately normal with mean 86 and standard deviation 9. What proportion of values are greater than 101.3?

options.why: Use the normal distribution's area, not the z-score.
That is the other side of the boundary.
Divide by σ when standardizing.

questions.stem: A test of H₀: p = 0.4 versus Hₐ: p > 0.4 gives a p-value of 0.03. Which interpretation is correct?

options.text: If p = 0.4, there is a 0.03 probability of a sample proportion at least as large as the one observed, by chance alone
options.why: Correct. That is the definition of the p-value.

options.text: There is a 0.97 probability that Hₐ is true
options.why: Not a valid interpretation.

options.text: There is a 0.03 probability that H₀ is true
options.why: A p-value is not the probability of a hypothesis.
Unrelated to the p-value.

questions.explanation: That is the definition of the p-value.

questions.stem: The data are: 13, 21, 23, 25, 27, 36, 38, 39, 68. Using the 1.5 × IQR rule, which statement is correct?

options.text: Q1 = 22, Q3 = 38.5; values above 63.3 are outliers, so 68 is an outlier
options.why: Correct. IQR = 16.5; upper fence = Q3 + 1.5·IQR = 63.3.

options.text: Q1 = 22, Q3 = 38.5; values above 55 are outliers, so 68 is an outlier
options.why: The fence uses 1.5 × IQR, not 1 × IQR.

options.text: There are no outliers because every value is within 2 standard deviations of the mean
options.why: The 1.5 × IQR rule is the method asked for.

options.text: Q1 = 22, Q3 = 38.5; values above 51.8 are outliers
options.why: Add 1.5·IQR to Q3, not to the median.

questions.stem: The data are: 10, 13, 17, 17, 19, 21, 24, 27, 30, 31, 33, 63. Using the 1.5 × IQR rule, which statement is correct?

options.text: There are no outliers because every value is within 2 standard deviations of the mean
options.why: The 1.5 × IQR rule is the method asked for.

options.text: Q1 = 17, Q3 = 30.5; values above 42.8 are outliers
options.why: Add 1.5·IQR to Q3, not to the median.

options.text: Q1 = 17, Q3 = 30.5; values above 50.8 are outliers, so 63 is an outlier
options.why: Correct. IQR = 13.5; upper fence = Q3 + 1.5·IQR = 50.8.

options.text: Q1 = 17, Q3 = 30.5; values above 44 are outliers, so 63 is an outlier
options.why: The fence uses 1.5 × IQR, not 1 × IQR.

questions.stem: Two independent random samples have n₁ = 55, s₁ = 6 and n₂ = 58, s₂ = 9. What is the standard error of x̄₁ − x̄₂?

options.why: Correct. √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂).
Variances add, even for a difference.
Each sample contributes s²/n.
Add variances, then take the square root; standard errors do not add.

questions.stem: The regression line is ŷ = 14 − 2.3x. An observation has x = 7 and y = -4.8. What is its residual, and what does it mean?

options.text: -2.7; the actual value is above the predicted value
options.why: A positive residual means the point is above the line.
That is the predicted value ŷ.

options.text: 2.7; the actual value is above the predicted value
options.why: Residual = actual − predicted, not predicted − actual.

options.text: -2.7; the actual value is below the predicted value
options.why: Correct. Residual = y − ŷ.

questions.stem: In an experiment on a new reading program, students are first grouped by reading level, then randomly assigned to programs within each level. What is the purpose of grouping by level?

options.why: It remains an experiment.

options.text: Blocking, to reduce variability caused by reading level
options.why: Correct. Blocking controls a known source of variation.
Groups by level are not placebo groups.
That is a sampling idea.

questions.explanation: Blocking controls a known source of variation.

questions.stem: A radio station asks listeners to call in with their opinions about a new law. Which type of bias is most likely?

options.why: The question wording is not the main issue.
Correct. People with strong opinions are more likely to call.

options.text: No bias, because listeners chose freely
options.why: Self-selection causes bias.
The main problem is self-selection.

questions.explanation: People with strong opinions are more likely to call.

questions.stem: What is the expected value of X?

options.why: That is the largest probability, not the mean.
That is the most likely value (mode), not the mean.
Weight each value by its probability.
Correct. μ = Σ x·P(x).

questions.stem: The correlation between height and arm span is r = 0.95. Which is a correct interpretation of r²?

options.text: About 95% of the variation in arm span is accounted for by the model
options.why: Square r.
Regression does not establish causation.

options.text: About 90.3% of the predictions are correct
options.why: r² is about variation explained, not accuracy of individual predictions.

options.text: About 90.3% of the variation in arm span is accounted for by the linear model relating arm span to height
options.why: Correct. r² is the proportion of variation in y explained by the linear model.

questions.stem: For a distribution of home prices in a county, the mean is 35 and the median is 41. Which is the most likely shape?

options.why: The mean is pulled toward the tail.
A uniform distribution is symmetric, with mean near the median.
Correct. A long left tail pulls the mean below the median.
In a symmetric distribution, the mean and median are close.

questions.explanation: Mean 35 < median 41: the mean is pulled toward the left tail.

questions.stem: The data are: 10, 10, 15, 16, 18, 18, 23, 24, 25, 25, 31, 40, 55. Using the 1.5 × IQR rule, which statement is correct?

options.text: Q1 = 15.5, Q3 = 28; values above 41.8 are outliers
options.why: Add 1.5·IQR to Q3, not to the median.

options.text: Q1 = 15.5, Q3 = 28; values above 40.5 are outliers, so 55 is an outlier
options.why: The fence uses 1.5 × IQR, not 1 × IQR.

options.text: Q1 = 15.5, Q3 = 28; values above 46.8 are outliers, so 55 is an outlier
options.why: Correct. IQR = 12.5; upper fence = Q3 + 1.5·IQR = 46.8.

options.text: There are no outliers because every value is within 2 standard deviations of the mean
options.why: The 1.5 × IQR rule is the method asked for.

questions.stem: For a distribution of home prices in a county, the mean is 51 and the median is 41. Which is the most likely shape?

options.why: In a symmetric distribution, the mean and median are close.
Correct. A long right tail pulls the mean above the median.
The mean is pulled toward the tail.
A uniform distribution is symmetric, with mean near the median.

questions.explanation: Mean 51 > median 41: the mean is pulled toward the right tail.

questions.stem: For a distribution of time spent on homework, the mean is 36 and the median is 45. Which is the most likely shape?

options.why: In a symmetric distribution, the mean and median are close.
The mean is pulled toward the tail.
A uniform distribution is symmetric, with mean near the median.
Correct. A long left tail pulls the mean below the median.

questions.explanation: Mean 36 < median 45: the mean is pulled toward the left tail.

questions.stem: Each of 9 independent devices fails with probability 0.08. What is the probability that at least one fails?

options.why: That is the probability none fail.
Probabilities of overlapping events cannot simply be added.
Correct. 1 − P(none fail) = 1 − (1 − p)^n.
That is the probability all fail.

questions.stem: A principal divides students by grade level and takes a simple random sample of 25 students from each grade. What sampling method is this?

options.why: Correct. SRSs within groups (strata).
Cluster sampling selects whole groups.
The selection is random.
That selects every kth individual.

questions.stem: What is the expected value of X?

options.why: Weight each value by its probability.
That is the most likely value (mode), not the mean.
Correct. μ = Σ x·P(x).
That is the largest probability, not the mean.

questions.stem: In a random sample of 270 customers of an online store, 154 would recommend it to a friend. Which is a 99% confidence interval for the proportion of all customers of an online store who would recommend it to a friend?

options.why: Correct. p̂ ± z*√(p̂(1 − p̂)/n) with z* = 2.576.
Divide by n inside the square root.
Use z* for 99%, not 1.96.
Use the standard error, √(p̂(1 − p̂)/n).

questions.stem: P(A) = 0.3, P(B) = 0.6 and P(A and B) = 0.15. What is P(A or B), and are A and B independent?

options.why: Correct. P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B); independent if P(A and B) = P(A)P(B) = 0.18.
Compare P(A and B) with P(A)·P(B) = 0.18.
Subtract P(A and B) so the overlap is not counted twice.
P(A and B) is not 0, so they are not mutually exclusive.

questions.stem: A sample of 12 values is used for a one-sample t interval. Which condition must be checked because the sample is small?

options.why: That is for chi-square tests.

options.text: The sample size is at least 30
options.why: That is the large-sample alternative.

options.text: The sample data show no strong skewness or outliers (population approximately normal)
options.why: Correct. Small samples need approximate normality.
That is for proportions.

questions.stem: Each of 7 independent trials succeeds with probability 0.6. What is the probability of exactly 6 successes?

options.why: Include the binomial coefficient and the failures.
Correct. Use the binomial distribution with n = 7 and p = 0.6.
Use p for successes, not 1 − p.
That is P(X ≤ k); the question asks for exactly k.

questions.stem: To test H₀: p = 0.6 versus Hₐ: p < 0.6, a random sample of 270 gives p̂ = 0.58. What are the test statistic and p-value?

options.why: The test's standard deviation uses p₀, not p̂.
The alternative is one-sided.
Find the area in the direction of Hₐ.
Correct. z = (p̂ − p₀)/√(p₀(1 − p₀)/n); one-sided p-value.

questions.stem: A random sample of 38 gives x̄ = 68.1 and s = 27. Test H₀: μ = 79 versus Hₐ: μ < 79. What are the test statistic and p-value?

options.why: The alternative is one-sided.
Correct. t = (x̄ − μ₀)/(s/√n) with df = n − 1.
Use the t distribution, not the normal.
Divide by the standard error s/√n.

questions.stem: A random sample of 39 has mean 76.7 and standard deviation 11.5. Which is a 90% confidence interval for the population mean?

options.why: Divide s by √n.
With s estimating σ, use t*, not z*.
Correct. x̄ ± t*·s/√n with t* = 1.686 (df = 38).
Divide by √n, not n.

questions.stem: In a randomized experiment, 96 of 240 subjects improved with treatment 1 and 183 of 300 improved with treatment 2. For a test of H₀: p₁ − p₂ = 0, what is the test statistic?

options.why: Use (1/n₁ + 1/n₂).
Correct. Pooled p̂c = 0.5167; z = (p̂₁ − p̂₂)/√(p̂c(1 − p̂c)(1/n₁ + 1/n₂)).
The test uses the pooled proportion, because H₀ assumes p₁ = p₂.
Divide the difference by its standard error.

questions.stem: To test H₀: p = 0.4 versus Hₐ: p < 0.4, a random sample of 350 gives p̂ = 0.37. What are the test statistic and p-value?

options.why: The alternative is one-sided.
Find the area in the direction of Hₐ.
The test's standard deviation uses p₀, not p̂.
Correct. z = (p̂ − p₀)/√(p₀(1 − p₀)/n); one-sided p-value.

questions.stem: To test H₀: p = 0.6 versus Hₐ: p > 0.6, a random sample of 240 gives p̂ = 0.63. What are the test statistic and p-value?

options.why: The test's standard deviation uses p₀, not p̂.
Correct. z = (p̂ − p₀)/√(p₀(1 − p₀)/n); one-sided p-value.
Find the area in the direction of Hₐ.
The alternative is one-sided.

questions.stem: Researchers recruited 200 volunteers among customers of the store and asked which of two study apps they already use, then compared test scores. Can the researchers conclude that the app causes higher scores, and to whom do the results apply?

options.text: Yes to cause and effect, and yes to generalizing to all customers of the store
options.why: Random assignment allows causal conclusions; random selection allows generalization to the population.

options.text: Yes to cause and effect, but only for the volunteers in the study
options.why: Random assignment allows causal conclusions; random selection allows generalization to the population.

options.text: No to cause and effect, and no generalization beyond the volunteers
options.why: Correct. No random assignment decides causation; no random selection decides generalization.

options.text: No to cause and effect, but the association can be generalized to all customers of the store
options.why: Random assignment allows causal conclusions; random selection allows generalization to the population.

questions.explanation: Random assignment: no. Random selection: no.

questions.stem: X and Y are independent with μX = 27, σX = 2, μY = 37, σY = 2. What are the mean and standard deviation of X + Y?

options.why: Check the sign of the mean.
That is the variance; take the square root.
Standard deviations do not add; variances do.
Correct. Means add or subtract; variances add.

questions.stem: If the sample size quadruples, what happens to the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of x̄?

options.text: It is cut to one quarter
options.why: It depends on √n.
Correct. σ/√n: √4 = 2.
It depends on n.
Larger samples reduce variability.

questions.stem: For a set of data, x̄ = 41, sx = 14, ȳ = 77, sy = 36 and r = 0.9. What is the least-squares regression line?

options.why: Correct. b = r·sy/sx and a = ȳ − b·x̄.
Multiply sy/sx by r.
The slope is r·sy/sx, not r·sx/sy.
a = ȳ − b·x̄.

questions.stem: A population has mean 75 and standard deviation 18 (shape unknown). For random samples of 40, what is the approximate probability that the sample mean exceeds 80.1?

options.why: Use σ/√n for a sample mean.
Divide σ by √n, not n.
That is the area below.
Correct. By the CLT, x̄ is approximately normal with SD 18/√40 = 2.846.

questions.stem: A random sample of 12 gives x̄ = 58.9 and s = 27. Test H₀: μ = 76 versus Hₐ: μ < 76. What are the test statistic and p-value?

options.why: Divide by the standard error s/√n.
Correct. t = (x̄ − μ₀)/(s/√n) with df = n − 1.
Use the t distribution, not the normal.
The alternative is one-sided.

questions.stem: What is the smallest sample size needed to estimate a proportion with a margin of error of at most 0.04 at 99% confidence, with no prior estimate of p?

options.why: Multiply by p̂(1 − p̂) = 0.25.
Square z*/m.
Always round up to guarantee the margin.
Correct. n ≥ (z*/m)²(0.5)(0.5) with z* = 2.576, rounded up.

questions.stem: For a chi-square test of homogeneity on these counts, what are the test statistic and degrees of freedom?

options.why: Do not divide by the total.
Do not take a square root.
For a two-way table, df = (r − 1)(c − 1).
Correct. χ² = Σ(O − E)²/E with df = (rows − 1)(columns − 1).

questions.stem: In a randomized experiment, 61 of 180 subjects improved with treatment 1 and 100 of 200 improved with treatment 2. For a test of H₀: p₁ − p₂ = 0, what is the test statistic?

options.why: Divide the difference by its standard error.
Use (1/n₁ + 1/n₂).
The test uses the pooled proportion, because H₀ assumes p₁ = p₂.
Correct. Pooled p̂c = 0.4237; z = (p̂₁ − p̂₂)/√(p̂c(1 − p̂c)(1/n₁ + 1/n₂)).

questions.stem: Assuming the null hypothesis of a chi-square test is true, what is the expected count for Group 1, Option A?

options.why: Expected counts depend on the row and column totals.
Divide by the table total once.
That is the observed count.
Correct. Expected = (row total × column total) / table total.

questions.stem: In a randomized experiment, 74 of 240 subjects improved with treatment 1 and 75 of 170 improved with treatment 2. For a test of H₀: p₁ − p₂ = 0, what is the test statistic?

options.why: Correct. Pooled p̂c = 0.3634; z = (p̂₁ − p̂₂)/√(p̂c(1 − p̂c)(1/n₁ + 1/n₂)).
The test uses the pooled proportion, because H₀ assumes p₁ = p₂.
Use (1/n₁ + 1/n₂).
Divide the difference by its standard error.

parts.prompt: Write an investigative question for this study, and identify the explanatory and response variables.

rubric.criterion: A clear investigative question that names the population or units and the variables.
rubric.example: "Does the mindfulness exercise lead to a better score on the next unit test than a reading break for units like these?"
Explanatory: treatment (the mindfulness exercise vs a reading break). Response: score on the next unit test.

parts.prompt: Explain why an experiment, rather than an observational study, should be used to answer the question.

rubric.criterion: Only random assignment allows a cause-and-effect conclusion; an observational study could be confounded.
rubric.example: Units that choose a treatment may differ in other ways that affect the response.

parts.prompt: Describe how to randomly assign the 80 units to the two treatments in a completely randomized design.

rubric.example: Number units 1–80; use a random number generator to select 40 different numbers.
Those 40 receive the mindfulness exercise; the remaining 40 receive a reading break.

parts.prompt: The researchers consider blocking by previous test average (high or low). Explain how blocking would be carried out and why it could improve the experiment.

rubric.criterion: Form blocks and randomize within each block.
rubric.example: Separate units into the blocks, then randomly assign half of each block to each treatment.

rubric.criterion: Benefit: reduces variability in the response due to the blocking variable, making a treatment effect easier to detect.
rubric.example: Accounts for differences caused by previous test average.

questions.title: Comparing reaction time (hundredths of a second)

parts.prompt: Find the five-number summary for each group.
Use the 1.5 × IQR rule to determine whether Evening has any outliers. Show your work.

rubric.example: IQR = 13; upper fence = 33 + 1.5(13) = 52.5. Outlier(s): 60.

parts.prompt: Compare the distributions of the two groups (shape, center and variability) in context.

rubric.example: The median for Evening (25) is greater than for Morning (16).
Evening is more variable (IQR 13 vs 11).

rubric.criterion: Comments on shape or unusual features.
rubric.example: Evening has a high outlier, suggesting right skew.

parts.prompt: Which measure of center is more appropriate for Evening, the mean or the median? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Median, because it is resistant to the outlier or skew.
rubric.example: Mean 28.4 is pulled toward the high value; median 25 is not.

parts.prompt: State the hypotheses, defining the parameter.

rubric.criterion: Correct hypotheses with the parameter defined.
rubric.example: H₀: p = 0.4; Hₐ: p > 0.4, where p is the proportion of all district students who take public transit.

parts.prompt: Identify the appropriate procedure and check its conditions.

rubric.criterion: One-sample z test for a proportion.
rubric.example: Random sample stated.
350 is less than 10% of all students (assumed); np₀ = 140 and n(1 − p₀) = 210 are both at least 10.

parts.prompt: Calculate the test statistic and p-value.
State a conclusion in context at α = 0.05.

rubric.criterion: Correct decision linked to the p-value, in context.
rubric.example: Because 0.0032 is less than 0.05, reject H₀: convincing evidence that the proportion is greater than 0.4.

parts.prompt: Write the equation of the least-squares regression line, defining the variables.

rubric.example: ŷ = 15.9 − 1.2x, where ŷ is predicted price (thousands of dollars) and x is age of car (years).

parts.prompt: Interpret the slope and the value of R-Sq in context.

rubric.example: For each additional unit of age of car (years), the predicted price (thousands of dollars) decreases by about 1.2.
About 89.0% of the variation in price (thousands of dollars) is accounted for by the linear model with age of car (years).

parts.prompt: One observation has x = 3 and y = 14.7. Calculate and interpret its residual. Also find the correlation r.

rubric.example: ŷ = 12.3; residual = 14.7 − 12.3 = 2.4: the actual value is above the prediction.

parts.prompt: The data come from a convenience sample. Explain how this affects the conclusions and describe a better data collection method.

rubric.criterion: Results may not generalize to the population; a random sample would allow generalization.
rubric.example: Take a simple random sample of used cars from the population of interest. Observational data also cannot show causation.
